questions.q: A complex number has modulus 2√2 and argument π/4. What is it?
questions.x: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = 2√2(1/√2 + i/√2) = 2 + 2i. Check: |2 + 2i| = √8 = 2√2, and the point (2, 2) lies on the line y = x in the first quadrant.

questions.q: A and B are subsets of a universal set U, and ′ denotes the complement. Which set equals (A ∪ B)′?
questions.x: By De Morgan's law the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. A′ ∪ B′ is the complement of A ∩ B instead.

questions.q: What is the value of log₅125 + log₂(1/4)?
questions.x: 125 = 5³ and 1/4 = 2⁻², so the sum is 3 + (−2) = 1. Taking log₂(1/4) as +2 gives 5.

questions.q: Which condition says exactly that a function f: A → B is onto?
o: the range of f is the whole of B
different elements of A have different images
the domain and co-domain have the same number of elements
every element of A has an image in B
questions.x: f is onto when every element of B is the image of some element of A, i.e. the range of f equals B. Different elements having different images is the one-one condition; every element of A having an image is true of any function.
The nth partial sum is 1 − 1/2ⁿ, and 1/2ⁿ → 0, so the limit is 1. Check: the sums 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, … approach 1. The value 2 belongs to the series that starts with 1.

questions.q: Cramer's rule is applied to two linear equations in x and y. The coefficient determinant D is 0 but Dₓ ≠ 0. What does this mean?
o: the system has a unique solution
the system has infinitely many solutions
questions.x: Any solution would satisfy D·x = Dₓ, i.e. 0 = Dₓ, which is false, so the system is inconsistent. Infinitely many solutions need D = Dₓ = Dᵧ = 0; a unique solution needs D ≠ 0.

questions.q: Completing the square turns x² − 8x + c = 0 into (x − 4)² = 5. What is the value of c?
questions.x: (x − 4)² = 5 expands to x² − 8x + 16 − 5 = 0, so c = 11. Check: x² − 8x + 11 = 0 has roots 4 ± √5. Adding 16 and 5 instead of subtracting gives 21.

questions.q: What is the vertex of the parabola y = x² − 6x + 5?
questions.x: y = (x − 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4, so the vertex is (3, −4). Check: x = −b/(2a) = 6/2 = 3 and y(3) = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4. Reading (x − 3)² as x = −3 gives (−3, −4).

questions.q: The 3rd term of a G.P. is 2. What is the product of its first five terms?
questions.x: The first five terms are a₃/r², a₃/r, a₃, a₃r, a₃r², whose product is a₃⁵ = 2⁵ = 32. Check with 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8: product 32. Adding instead of multiplying the powers gives 10.

questions.q: Nonzero numbers a, b, c are such that 1/a, 1/b, 1/c form an A.P. with nonzero common difference. Then a, b, c form
o: both an A.P. and a G.P.
questions.x: By definition a sequence is harmonic when the reciprocals of its terms are in A.P., so a, b, c are in H.P. For example 1/a, 1/b, 1/c = 1, 2, 3 gives 1, 1/2, 1/3, which is neither an A.P. nor a G.P.

questions.q: For events E and F, P(E) = 0.5, P(F) = 0.4 and P(E ∩ F) = 0.2. Which statement is true?
o: E and F are mutually exclusive
The probability that neither happens is 0.2
questions.x: P(E)P(F) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 = P(E ∩ F), so E and F are independent. E and F are not mutually exclusive since P(E ∩ F) ≠ 0. P(E ∪ F) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7, so neither happens with probability 0.3.

questions.q: For every positive integer n, 10ⁿ + 3·4^(n + 2) + 5 is divisible by:
questions.x: n = 1 gives 10 + 192 + 5 = 207 = 9 × 23, which 27, 7 and 11 do not divide. In the inductive step, 10^(k+1) + 3·4^(k+3) + 5 = 10[10ᵏ + 3·4^(k+2) + 5] − 18·4^(k+2) − 45, and both extra terms are multiples of 9.

questions.q: For angles where it is defined, (1 + tan²θ)/(1 + cot²θ) simplifies to:
questions.x: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, so the quotient is sec²θ/cosec²θ = sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ. Check θ = 45°: 2/2 = 1 = tan²45°, and at θ = 60°: 4/(4/3) = 3 = tan²60°.

questions.q: For angles where it is defined, cot(A + B) equals:
o: (cot A cot B − 1)/(cot A + cot B)
(cot A cot B + 1)/(cot A + cot B)
(cot A + cot B)/(cot A cot B − 1)
(1 − cot A cot B)/(cot A + cot B)
questions.x: cot(A + B) = cos(A + B)/sin(A + B) = (cos A cos B − sin A sin B)/(sin A cos B + cos A sin B); dividing top and bottom by sin A sin B gives (cot A cot B − 1)/(cot A + cot B). (cot A cot B + 1)/(cot B − cot A) would be cot(A − B).

questions.q: For angles where it is defined, (1 − cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ) equals:
questions.x: 1 − cos 2θ = 2 sin²θ and 1 + cos 2θ = 2 cos²θ, so the quotient is tan²θ. Swapping the two half-angle forms gives cot²θ.

questions.q: What is the domain of y = sec x? (k ∈ ℤ)
o: all real x except x = kπ
questions.x: sec x = 1/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0, that is at odd multiples of π/2. The points x = kπ are excluded for cosec x and cot x, where sin x = 0.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 4, B = 30° and C = 45°. What is the area of the triangle?
questions.x: A = 105° and sin 105° = (√6 + √2)/4. Δ = a² sin B sin C/(2 sin A) = 16 × ½ × (√2/2) ÷ ((√6 + √2)/2) = 8/(√3 + 1) = 4(√3 − 1). Leaving out the 2 in the denominator gives 8(√3 − 1).

questions.q: The graph of y = cos⁻¹x meets the x-axis at the point:
questions.x: On the x-axis y = 0, and cos⁻¹x = 0 only when x = cos 0 = 1. The graph starts at (−1, π) and falls to (1, 0); (0, 0) is where y = sin⁻¹x crosses.

questions.q: On the curve y = x², at which value x = a is the tangent parallel to the chord joining the points where x = 1 and x = 5?
questions.x: Chord slope = (25 − 1)/(5 − 1) = 6. The tangent slope is 2a, so 2a = 6 and a = 3. Answering 6 confuses the slope with the point.

questions.q: What are the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series of cosh x?
questions.x: cosh x = ½(eˣ + e⁻ˣ): the odd powers cancel and the even ones stay, all positive, giving 1 + x²/2! + x⁴/4!. The alternating signs belong to cos x, and x + x³/6 + ... is sinh x.

questions.q: The derivative of f at x = a is defined as:
questions.x: f′(a) is the limit of the slope of the chord from (a, f(a)) to (x, f(x)), i.e. lim(x→a) [f(x) − f(a)]/(x − a). The symmetric quotient over h (not 2h) gives 2f′(a), and lim [f(x) − f(a)] is 0 for any continuous f.

questions.q: f is continuous and ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 6. What is ∫₀¹ f(3x) dx?
questions.x: Put u = 3x, du = 3 dx; x from 0 to 1 gives u from 0 to 3, so ∫₀¹ f(3x) dx = (1/3)∫₀³ f(u) du = 6/3 = 2. Multiplying by 3 instead gives 18.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the parabola y = x² and the line y = x + 2 is:
questions.x: They meet where x² = x + 2, i.e. x = −1 and x = 2, and the line is above. Area = ∫₋₁² (x + 2 − x²) dx = (2 + 4 − 8/3) − (½ − 2 + 1/3) = 10/3 + 7/6 = 9/2. Using only the upper limit gives 10/3.

questions.q: Eliminating the constants m and c from y = mx + c gives which differential equation?
questions.x: dy/dx = m, and differentiating again gives d²y/dx² = 0. dy/dx = m still contains a constant, so it is not the required equation.

questions.q: The points (1, 2) and (3, k) are at the same distance from the line y = x. What are the possible values of k?
questions.x: The distance from (x, y) to x − y = 0 is |x − y|/√2. So |3 − k| = |1 − 2| = 1, giving k = 2 or k = 4. Missing the case 3 − k = 1 leaves only 4.

questions.q: A workshop makes x chairs and y tables. A chair needs 1 hour of polishing and a table 2 hours; at most 10 hours are available and at most 6 chairs can be made. Profit is Rs 40 per chair and Rs 100 per table. What is the maximum profit?
questions.x: Constraints: x + 2y ≤ 10, x ≤ 6, x, y ≥ 0. Corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 2), (0, 5) give 0, 240, 440 and 500, so the maximum is Rs 500 at (0, 5). Rs 640 needs (6, 4), which uses 14 hours.

questions.q: What are the ends of the major axis (the vertices) of the ellipse x²/9 + y²/25 = 1?
questions.x: 25 > 9, so the major axis is along the y-axis with a = 5: vertices (0, ±5). (0, ±4) are the foci, since c² = 25 − 9 = 16.

questions.q: Which of these lines does NOT meet the hyperbola x²/4 − y²/9 = 1?
questions.x: y = 3x/2 is an asymptote: substituting gives x²/4 − x²/4 = 1, which is impossible. y = x gives x²(1/4 − 1/9) = 1, y = 0 gives x = ±2 and x = 3 gives y² = 45/4, so those lines all meet it.

questions.q: What is the sine of the angle between a = i + j and b = j + k?
questions.x: a × b = i − j + k, of magnitude √3, and |a||b| = √2 × √2 = 2, so sin θ = √3/2. Check: cos θ = a · b/2 = ½, so θ = 60°.

questions.q: f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a)·f(b) < 0. What can be concluded?
o: f(x) = 0 has at least one root between a and b
f(x) = 0 has exactly one root between a and b
f(x) = 0 has no root between a and b
f(x) = 0 has a root only at a or at b
questions.x: f changes sign between a and b, and a continuous function cannot change sign without passing through 0, so there is at least one root in between. There may be more than one, for example three.

questions.q: How many base units does the SI system have?
questions.x: The SI has seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Six is the usual slip of forgetting the candela or the mole.

questions.q: A force F acts along the positive y-axis at a point whose position vector from the origin lies along the positive x-axis. The direction of the torque τ = r × F about the origin is:
questions.x: τ = r × F has the direction of î × ĵ = k̂, the positive z-axis, by the right-hand rule. Taking F × r instead gives −z; the torque is perpendicular to both r and F, never along either.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of its flight the ball has:
o: Zero velocity and an acceleration g downward
Zero velocity and an acceleration g upward
questions.x: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, but gravity still acts, so its acceleration is g vertically downward throughout. Believing zero velocity means zero acceleration is the classic error.

questions.q: Two bodies of equal mass, one moving due east at 3 m s⁻¹ and the other due north at 4 m s⁻¹, collide and stick together. Their common speed just after the collision is:
questions.x: Total momentum = √((3m)² + (4m)²) = 5m, shared by mass 2m, so the speed is 5m/2m = 2.5 m s⁻¹. Averaging the two speeds as if they were in the same direction gives 3.5 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, a body is to be launched vertically upward from the Earth's surface so that it just reaches a height equal to the Earth's radius R. With g = 10 m s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the launch speed needed is:
questions.x: ½mv² = GMm/R − GMm/2R = GMm/2R = ½mgR, so v = √(gR) = √(6.4 × 10⁷) = 8 × 10³ m s⁻¹ = 8 km s⁻¹. Using mgh with h = R (constant g) gives √(2gR) = 8√2 km s⁻¹, the escape velocity, which is too large.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance and the Earth's rotation, the escape velocity of a body launched from the Earth's surface:
o: Is least when it is launched vertically upward
Is least when it is launched horizontally
Does not depend on the direction in which it is launched
Is greatest when it is launched at 45°
questions.x: Escape depends only on energy: ½mv² must equal GMm/R. Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the same speed is needed in any direction (as long as the path does not hit the Earth). Thinking of it like a projectile range is the slip.

questions.q: A wheel starts from rest and turns with uniform angular acceleration. In the first 10 s it turns through 100 rad. Through what angle does it turn in the next 10 s?
questions.x: From rest θ = ½αt², so θ ∝ t²: in 20 s it turns 4 × 100 = 400 rad, so in the second 10 s it turns 400 − 100 = 300 rad (check: α = 2 rad s⁻²). 400 rad is the total for 20 s; 100 rad assumes constant angular velocity.

questions.q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 3 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of cross-sectional area 4 cm². The mass of water passing any cross-section each second is:
questions.x: Volume per second = Av = 4 × 10⁻⁴ × 3 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³, so mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 1.2 × 10⁻³ = 1.2 kg. Converting 4 cm² as 4 × 10⁻² m² gives 120 kg.

questions.q: A 0.1 kg mass performs SHM with angular frequency 20 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.05 m. Its total energy is:
questions.x: E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.1 × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.05 J (check: v_max = ωx₀ = 1 m s⁻¹ and ½mv² = 0.05 J). Forgetting the ½ gives 0.1 J; not squaring ω gives 0.0025 J.

questions.q: Crests of a water wave travel 12 m in 3 s, and neighbouring crests are 0.5 m apart. The frequency of the wave is:
questions.x: v = 12/3 = 4 m s⁻¹ and λ = 0.5 m, so f = v/λ = 4/0.5 = 8 Hz. Multiplying v by λ gives 2; dividing the distance 12 m directly by λ gives 24.

questions.q: An air column in a pipe closed at one end can resonate at:
questions.x: A closed end must be a node and an open end an antinode, so the length must be an odd number of quarter wavelengths, L = (2n − 1)λ/4, giving only odd harmonics. All harmonics occur in a pipe open at both ends.

questions.q: A Young's double-slit experiment is done with white light. The central fringe is white. In the first-order coloured fringe on each side, which colour lies closest to the central fringe?
questions.x: The position of the first bright fringe is y = λL/d, which is proportional to the wavelength. Violet has the shortest wavelength, so it lies nearest the centre and red lies farthest out.

questions.q: An insect 2 mm long is viewed with a magnifying glass of magnifying power 10. Without the lens it would be viewed at the near point, 25 cm away. What angle does its image subtend at the eye through the lens?
questions.x: Unaided angle = 0.002 m/0.25 m = 0.008 rad. Magnifying power is the ratio of angles, so the image subtends 10 × 0.008 = 0.08 rad. Stopping at the unaided angle gives 0.008 rad.

questions.q: A Carnot engine of efficiency 40% absorbs 500 J of heat from its source in each cycle and completes 5 cycles per second. Its power output is:
questions.x: Work per cycle = 0.40 × 500 = 200 J; with 5 cycles per second the power is 200 × 5 = 1000 W. 200 W is the work in one cycle; 1500 W is the heat rejected per second.

questions.q: When a gas is heated at constant volume, the heat supplied:
o: All goes into work done by the gas
Is shared equally between work and internal energy
Is all lost to the surroundings
All goes to increase its internal energy
questions.x: At constant volume ΔV = 0, so no work is done and Q = ΔU: all the heat raises the internal energy.

questions.q: A 5 μF capacitor holds a charge of 50 μC. The energy stored in it is:
questions.x: U = Q²/2C = (50 × 10⁻⁶)²/(2 × 5 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ J. Check: V = Q/C = 10 V and ½QV = ½ × 50 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ J. Leaving out the ½ gives 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ J.

questions.q: Between two large, parallel metal plates with equal and opposite charges, away from the edges, the electric field lines are:
o: Parallel and equally spaced, from the negative plate to the positive plate
Parallel and equally spaced, from the positive plate to the negative plate, showing a uniform field
Curved, and closest together midway between the plates
Radial, spreading out from the centre of the positive plate
questions.x: Between large oppositely charged plates the field has the same size and direction everywhere (E = σ/ε₀), so its lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced. Field lines always run from positive to negative charge.

questions.q: A wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm² has a resistance of 4 Ω. The conductivity of its material is:
questions.x: ρ = RA/L = 4 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, and conductivity σ = 1/ρ = 1 × 10⁶ S m⁻¹. Writing the resistivity's number with the conductivity unit gives 1 × 10⁻⁶ S m⁻¹.

questions.q: A 9 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination. One branch of the combination is a 6 Ω resistor; the other branch is a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor in series. The p.d. across the 4 Ω resistor is:
questions.x: The branches are 6 Ω and 6 Ω, so the combination is 3 Ω; the total is 6 Ω and I = 1.5 A. The p.d. across the combination is 4.5 V, so the 2 Ω + 4 Ω branch carries 0.75 A and the 4 Ω resistor has 0.75 × 4 = 3 V. 4.5 V is the p.d. across the whole branch.

questions.q: An electron moves at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at an angle of 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The magnetic force on it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° ≈ 0.87):
questions.x: F = evB sin θ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁶ × 0.5 × 0.5 = 8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Leaving out sin 30° gives 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N; using cos 30° gives about 1.4 × 10⁻¹³ N.

questions.q: A 50-turn coil of area 0.04 m² lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. It is turned over through 180° in 0.1 s. The average emf induced in it is:
questions.x: The flux per turn goes from +BA = +0.02 Wb to −0.02 Wb, a change of 0.04 Wb. So ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 50 × 0.04/0.1 = 20 V. Taking the change as just BA (as for a 90° turn) gives 10 V; seeing the same magnitude at the start and end gives zero.

questions.q: The flux through each turn of a 10-turn coil rises steadily from 0 to 0.06 Wb in 0.2 s and then stays at 0.06 Wb. The induced emf during the first 0.2 s and after it is, respectively:
questions.x: While the flux changes, ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 10 × 0.06/0.2 = 3 V; once the flux is constant, ε = 0. Forgetting the 10 turns gives 0.3 V; thinking a large steady flux still induces an emf gives 3 V then 3 V.

questions.q: In an AC circuit, the voltage is v = 200 sin(ωt + π/3) V and the current is i = 5 sin(ωt − π/6) A. The phase relation between them is:
o: The current leads the voltage by 90°
The voltage leads the current by 30°
The voltage leads the current by 90°
questions.x: The phase difference is π/3 − (−π/6) = π/3 + π/6 = π/2 = 90°, with the voltage ahead, as in a pure inductor. Subtracting π/6 from π/3 instead (ignoring the minus sign) gives 30°.

questions.q: Tensile strain is defined as the change in length divided by the original length. The SI unit of strain is:
questions.x: Strain = ΔL/L is metres divided by metres, a pure ratio with no unit. N m⁻² is the unit of stress (and of the moduli), not of strain.

questions.q: An inverting amplifier has an input resistor of 1 kΩ and a feedback resistor of 20 kΩ. The op-amp is powered from a ±9 V supply. A steady input of +1 V is applied. The output voltage is about:
questions.x: The ideal formula gives V_out = −(20/1) × 1 = −20 V, but the output cannot go beyond the supply voltages, so the op-amp saturates at about −9 V. Using the formula without the supply limit gives −20 V; using 1 + R₂/R₁ gives −21 V.

questions.q: The first postulate of the special theory of relativity states that:
o: The speed of light depends on the speed of its source
Every frame of reference is an inertial frame
Time passes at the same rate for all observers
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference
questions.x: The first postulate (principle of relativity) says that all inertial frames are equivalent: the laws of physics take the same form in each. The second postulate is about the constant speed of light, which does not depend on the source's speed.

questions.q: To explain the black-body spectrum, Planck assumed that the oscillating atoms of the body can emit or absorb energy:
o: Only in whole-number multiples of hf
questions.x: Planck's hypothesis was that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets (quanta), so the energy of an oscillator of frequency f can only be E = nhf with n = 1, 2, 3, … The classical idea of continuous energy exchange is what failed.

questions.q: In a three-level laser, atoms are pumped from the ground state (0 eV) to a level at 3.0 eV, fall quickly to a metastable level at 2.0 eV, and then lase by falling from the metastable level to the ground state. The wavelength of the laser light is: (hc = 1240 eV nm)
questions.x: The laser transition is from 2.0 eV to 0 eV, so the photon energy is 2.0 eV and λ = 1240/2.0 = 620 nm. Using the pump energy 3.0 eV gives 413 nm; using the fast 3.0 → 2.0 eV drop gives 1240 nm; adding 3.0 and 2.0 eV gives 248 nm.

questions.q: A radioactive sample is left for a time equal to three of its half-lives. The fraction of the original nuclei that have decayed is:
questions.x: After 3 half-lives the fraction left is (½)³ = 1/8, so the fraction decayed is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. Giving the fraction remaining (1/8) instead of the fraction decayed is the usual slip.

questions.q: In an ultrasound probe, the same piezoelectric crystal acts both as the transmitter and as the receiver. It can receive because:
o: The echo heats the crystal and changes its resistance
A returning echo makes the crystal vibrate, and the stressed crystal produces a potential difference
The echo makes the crystal emit light
The crystal stores the outgoing pulse and compares it with the echo
questions.x: An alternating p.d. makes the crystal vibrate and send out ultrasound; an echo that squeezes and stretches the crystal makes it produce an alternating p.d. (the piezoelectric effect), which the machine detects. The same effect works both ways, so one crystal does both jobs.

questions.q: In the combustion analysis of an organic compound that contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, the percentage of oxygen is usually found by:
o: Weighing the oxygen absorbed by the magnesium perchlorate tube
Weighing the oxygen absorbed by the potash bulbs
Measuring the volume of oxygen gas given off
Subtracting the percentages of carbon and hydrogen from 100
questions.x: The absorbers only catch H₂O (magnesium perchlorate) and CO₂ (potash, KOH); oxygen is not measured directly, so %O = 100 − (%C + %H). Thinking that the absorbers trap oxygen is the usual slip.

questions.q: In fractional distillation of a mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water, a fractionating column is fitted because it:
o: Cools the vapour so that both liquids condense together
Gives a large surface on which vapour condenses and re-evaporates many times, so the vapour reaching the top is rich in ethanol
Stops the water from boiling at all
Raises the boiling point of ethanol above that of water
questions.x: Each condensation and re-evaporation on the column's packing enriches the vapour in the more volatile ethanol, so it separates two miscible liquids whose boiling points are not far apart. The column does not stop water boiling or change the boiling points.

questions.q: In the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, the units of the constant a are:
questions.x: an²/V² must have units of pressure, so a = P × V²/n² = atm dm⁶ mol⁻². dm³ mol⁻¹ is the unit of b, the volume correction.

questions.q: All crystals can be grouped into how many crystal systems?
questions.x: There are seven crystal systems: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal and rhombohedral (trigonal). 14 is the number of Bravais lattices and 6 is the number of unit-cell parameters.

questions.q: In an oil-drop experiment, the charges on four drops were found to be 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. These results are consistent with a charge on one electron of:
questions.x: Every charge must be a whole-number multiple of e: 3.2, 4.8, 8.0 and 6.4 are 2, 3, 5 and 4 times 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the smallest measured value but 4.8 is not a whole multiple of it; 5.6 is just the average.

questions.q: Bond energies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
questions.x: Bonds broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ; bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ released. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. +184 reverses the sign (formed minus broken), and +247 uses only one H–Cl bond.

questions.q: Metals such as copper and gold can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires without breaking. In terms of metallic bonding, this is because:
o: The metal atoms are held by strong directional covalent bonds that bend easily
The metal ions and electrons form a rigid lattice of oppositely charged ions like NaCl
Layers of positive metal ions can slide over one another while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together
The valence electrons are fixed between pairs of neighbouring metal ions
questions.x: In the electron-sea model the bonding is non-directional: when layers of ions slide, the delocalised electrons move with them and the attraction is kept, so the metal deforms instead of shattering. An ionic lattice shatters because sliding brings like charges together, which is the tempting but wrong comparison.

questions.q: A spirit lamp burns 0.46 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH, and the heat warms 200 g of water by 15 K. Assuming all the heat goes into the water (c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), what is the enthalpy of combustion of ethanol?
questions.x: q = 200 × 4.2 × 15 = 12 600 J = 12.6 kJ. M(C₂H₅OH) = 46 g mol⁻¹, so 0.46 g = 0.010 mol and ΔH = −12.6 ÷ 0.010 = −1260 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because heat is released). −12.6 kJ mol⁻¹ forgets to divide by the moles, and −27.4 divides by the mass in grams instead.

questions.q: At about what temperature is the converter run in the contact process, where SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ over V₂O₅?
questions.x: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature favours the yield but the reaction is then too slow; about 400–450 °C with the V₂O₅ catalyst gives a good rate and a high conversion. 1000 °C would give a fast rate but a poor equilibrium yield.

questions.q: Ksp of AgCl = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is the solubility of AgCl in 0.010 mol dm⁻³ NaCl solution?
questions.x: With [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.010 mol dm⁻³ from the NaCl, the solubility s = [Ag⁺] = Ksp ÷ [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³. 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ is the solubility in pure water, ignoring the common ion; 1.0 × 10⁻¹² multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: Equal masses of liquid X (molar mass 50 g mol⁻¹) and liquid Y (molar mass 100 g mol⁻¹) are mixed and form an ideal solution. At the temperature used, pure X has a vapour pressure of 60 kPa and pure Y 30 kPa. What is the vapour pressure of the solution?
questions.x: Take 100 g of each: 2 mol X and 1 mol Y, so x(X) = 2/3 and x(Y) = 1/3. P = (2/3)(60) + (1/3)(30) = 40 + 10 = 50 kPa. Treating equal masses as equal moles gives 45 kPa; 40 kPa is the partial pressure of X alone.

questions.q: E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V and E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. For the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ under standard conditions, what is E°cell and is the reaction feasible?
questions.x: Fe³⁺ is reduced (cathode) and I⁻ is oxidised (anode): E°cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V. A positive E°cell means the reaction is feasible. Adding the two potentials gives 1.31 V; E° values are not multiplied by the coefficients.

questions.q: In acid solution dichromate oxidises iodide: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + I⁻ + H⁺ → Cr³⁺ + I₂ + H₂O (not balanced). How many moles of I₂ are set free by 0.10 mol of Cr₂O₇²⁻?
questions.x: Each Cr goes from +6 to +3, so one Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains 6 electrons; each I₂ formed releases 2 electrons, so 3 I₂ form per Cr₂O₇²⁻: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6I⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3I₂ + 7H₂O. 0.10 mol gives 0.30 mol I₂. 0.60 mol is the iodide used, not the iodine formed.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction because it:
o: Makes ΔH of the reaction more negative
Increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules
Shifts the equilibrium position towards the products
Provides another pathway with a lower activation energy, leaving ΔH unchanged
questions.x: A catalyst offers an alternative route with a lower Ea, so more collisions are effective at the same temperature. It does not change ΔH, the energy of the molecules or the position of equilibrium.

questions.q: In each period of the periodic table, the element with the highest first ionisation energy is the:
o: Alkali metal at the start of the period
Noble gas at the end of the period
Element in the middle of the period
questions.x: Ionisation energy generally rises across a period as nuclear charge increases and the radius falls, and the noble gas has a stable, completely filled outer shell. The alkali metal has the lowest value.

questions.q: Magnesium carbonate is heated strongly. Besides carbon dioxide, which product is formed?
questions.x: MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂: Group 2 carbonates decompose to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide. No hydrogen is present, so a hydroxide cannot form, and the metal is not set free.

questions.q: In a sheet silicate such as mica or talc, each SiO₄ tetrahedron shares three of its oxygen atoms with neighbouring tetrahedra. The empirical formula of the silicate anion is:
questions.x: Each Si has one unshared O plus three shared O counted as half each: 1 + 3/2 = 5/2 O per Si, i.e. Si₂O₅; charge = 2(+4) + 5(−2) = −2. Sharing two oxygens (chains) gives SiO₃²⁻, the most tempting wrong option.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes red phosphorus from white phosphorus?
o: Red phosphorus is insoluble in carbon disulphide, whereas white phosphorus dissolves in it
Red phosphorus glows in the dark in moist air, whereas white phosphorus does not
Red phosphorus consists of discrete P₄ molecules, whereas white phosphorus is polymeric
Red phosphorus is highly poisonous, whereas white phosphorus is not
questions.x: Polymeric red phosphorus does not dissolve in CS₂, while molecular P₄ (white) does. The other statements are all reversed: white phosphorus glows, is molecular and is very poisonous.

questions.q: Transition metals and their compounds are often good catalysts mainly because they:
o: Show variable oxidation states and can adsorb reactants on their surfaces
questions.x: They can easily gain and lose electrons by changing oxidation state, and their partly filled d orbitals let reactants bond temporarily to the surface, lowering the activation energy. Partly filled, not completely filled, d subshells are the key.

questions.q: In catalytic reforming, n-hexane, C₆H₁₄, is converted into benzene, C₆H₆. How many moles of hydrogen are released per mole of hexane?
questions.x: C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₆ + xH₂; hydrogen balance: 14 = 6 + 2x, so x = 4 (ring closure removes one H₂ and forming three C=C removes three more). Thinking of only the three double bonds gives 3; using H atoms instead of H₂ molecules gives 8.

questions.q: Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, is classified as:
questions.x: Cyclohexane has a closed ring of carbon atoms only, with no benzene-type delocalised ring, so it is alicyclic (homocyclic, non-aromatic). Calling every six-membered ring aromatic is the tempting slip.

questions.q: The rates at which the halogens take part in free-radical substitution of methane follow the order:
questions.x: Reactivity falls down the group: fluorine reacts explosively, chlorine readily in light, bromine slowly, and iodine hardly at all. The reversed order mixes up reactivity with the ease of breaking the X–X bond alone.

questions.q: 15.6 g of benzene is converted completely into bromobenzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃. All the HBr formed is absorbed in water. What volume of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ NaOH neutralises it? (C₆H₆ = 78 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 15.6/78 = 0.20 mol benzene; C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr gives 0.20 mol HBr, which needs 0.20 mol NaOH: 0.20/0.50 = 0.40 dm³ = 400 cm³. Multiplying by 0.50 instead of dividing gives 100 cm³.

questions.q: The SN2 reaction of hydroxide ions with bromomethane, CH₃Br, has an overall order of:
questions.x: SN2 is one step in which OH⁻ and CH₃Br collide, so rate = k[CH₃Br][OH⁻], first order in each and second order overall. First order is the SN1 rate law, where only the alkyl halide appears.

questions.q: Methoxyethane, CH₃OC₂H₅, is treated with one mole of cold concentrated HI. The products are:
questions.x: HI protonates the ether oxygen, and I⁻ then attacks the less hindered carbon (SN2), the methyl group, so CH₃I and C₂H₅OH form. Both iodides form only with excess hot HI; iodoethane and methanol would need attack at the more crowded ethyl carbon.

questions.q: But-1-ene is absorbed in cold concentrated H₂SO₄ and the product is warmed with water. The alcohol formed is then oxidised with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. The final organic product is:
questions.x: Markovnikov addition puts –OH on carbon 2, giving butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, which oxidises to the ketone CH₃COCH₂CH₃. Butanal or butanoic acid would follow only if the –OH went to carbon 1 (anti-Markovnikov).

questions.q: In the α-amino acids found in proteins, the amino group is attached to:
o: The carbon atom of the –COOH group
The carbon atom next to the –COOH group
The carbon atom at the far end of the chain
The oxygen atom of the –COOH group
questions.x: α means the first carbon after the carboxyl carbon, so in H₂N–CHR–COOH the NH₂ and the side chain R share that carbon. Putting NH₂ on the carboxyl carbon itself would make an amide-like group, not an amino acid.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CN is:
questions.x: In nitrile names the carbon of –C≡N is counted in the chain, so the four-carbon chain gives butanenitrile. Leaving out the CN carbon gives propanenitrile, the most common slip; 2-methylpropanenitrile is the branched isomer.

questions.q: How many signals appear in the ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH?
questions.x: The three CH₃ groups are equivalent and give one signal (9H, a doublet); the single CH gives the second signal. Counting each CH₃ separately gives 4.

questions.q: In a catalytic converter, 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. What mass of nitrogen is formed when 5.6 g of CO reacts completely? (CO = 28 g mol⁻¹, N₂ = 28 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 5.6/28 = 0.20 mol CO gives 0.20/2 = 0.10 mol N₂ = 2.8 g. Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio gives 5.6 g, and 8.8 g is the mass of CO₂ formed.

questions.q: A shopkeeper saves the day's sales file on a USB drive so that he can use it again next week. Which stage of the information-processing cycle is this?
questions.x: Keeping data or results on a device for later use is the storage stage. Processing would be working out totals from the sales, which is not what saving the file does.

questions.q: Which of the following travels on the data bus?
o: The address of the memory location to be read
A 'memory write' signal from the control unit
An instruction being read from memory into the CPU
The ticks of the system clock
questions.x: The data bus carries the data and instructions themselves between the CPU, memory and input/output. The address goes on the address bus, and read/write and timing signals go on the control bus.

questions.q: A student who cannot use a keyboard gives commands to the computer by speaking. Which input device picks up his voice?
questions.x: A microphone turns sound into signals the computer can accept, so it is an input device. A speaker does the opposite: it is an output device that produces sound.

questions.q: A website address ending in .edu is generally used by:
questions.x: The .edu domain is used for educational institutions such as universities and colleges. Government sites use .gov and commercial companies typically use .com.

questions.q: What does FTP stand for?
questions.x: FTP is the File Transfer Protocol, a standard set of rules for copying files between computers over a network. The other expansions are not real protocol names.

questions.q: HTML is the:
o: Protocol that sends e-mail between servers
Language used to create and structure web pages
Address of a website's home page
questions.x: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses tags to mark up the headings, text, images and links of a web page. Sending e-mail between servers is the job of SMTP, not HTML.

questions.q: Why should the virus definitions of an antivirus program be updated regularly?
o: So that newly discovered viruses can be recognised
So that the computer starts up faster
So that forgotten passwords are reset
So that more space is free on the hard disk
questions.x: Antivirus software spots viruses by comparing files with a list of known virus signatures, so new viruses are missed until the list is updated. Updating does not speed up start-up or free disk space.

questions.q: A physical server has 64 GB of RAM. The hypervisor needs 4 GB of it, and each virtual machine is given 7 GB. What is the largest number of virtual machines it can run at once?
questions.x: 64 − 4 = 60 GB is left for virtual machines, and 60 ÷ 7 = 8 remainder 4, so 8 machines (56 GB) fit but a 9th (63 GB) does not. The answer 9 comes from forgetting the hypervisor's 4 GB (64 ÷ 7).

questions.q: In some blockchains such as Bitcoin, computers compete to solve a hard puzzle, and the winner adds the next block and earns a reward. This is called:
questions.x: Mining is the process of solving the puzzle (proof of work) to add and confirm a new block. Phishing is an online fraud, not part of a blockchain.

questions.q: A computer that is already running is restarted without switching off its power. This is called:
questions.x: A warm boot restarts the computer while the power stays on, for example with the Restart command. A cold boot starts the computer from power off.

questions.q: In mail merge, the document that holds the text that is the same in every letter, together with the merge fields, is called the:
questions.x: The main document has the fixed text and the places (merge fields) where each record's data goes. The data source is the separate list that supplies the names and addresses.

questions.q: After normalisation, Student(Roll, Name, ClassID) and Class(ClassID, Teacher) were made from one table. How can each student's name be shown with the class teacher?
o: Join the two tables on Name and Teacher
Copy Teacher back into every Student row
Add Roll to Class as a second key
Join the two tables on the common column ClassID
questions.x: The foreign key ClassID in Student matches the primary key of Class, so joining on it brings each student's row together with the class's teacher. Copying Teacher back would bring the redundancy back.

questions.q: Which statement about a table (relation) in the relational model is correct?
o: Rows must be stored in primary-key order
No two rows are exactly the same
One column may hold values of different types
Two columns may have the same name
questions.x: Each row of a relation is unique, which the primary key guarantees. The order of rows does not matter, every column takes values from one domain, and column names in a table are different.

questions.q: In database design, what is an entity?
o: A single value stored in one field of a record
A person, place, thing or event about which data is stored
A line that joins two shapes in a diagram
A rule that limits the values of a field
questions.x: An entity is something of interest to the organisation, such as Student or Book, about which data is kept. A single stored value is an attribute's value, and a rule on values is a constraint.

questions.q: A school logo must appear at the top of a form and stay the same for every record. Which control is used for it?
questions.x: An image control shows a fixed picture that does not depend on the record. A bound object frame shows a picture stored in a field of each record, so it changes from record to record.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a form in Access?
o: To print grouped totals on paper
To enter, view and edit data in a convenient layout
To define the data types of fields
questions.x: A form is a screen for working with records comfortably. The data itself is stored in tables, printed summaries are made with reports, and data types are set in table Design View.

questions.q: Which format specifier prints a value of type `long int`?
questions.x: The l modifier with d, %ld, is for long int. %lf is used with scanf for a double, and plain %d is for int.
%2d reads at most 2 digits, so a = 12; the next %d reads the remaining digits, so b = 345. Without the width, a would take all five digits.

questions.q: In a `while` loop, when is the condition tested?
o: After every execution of the body
Only once, before the first execution
Before every execution of the body
Only when a `break` statement is reached
questions.x: while is an entry-controlled loop: the condition is checked before each pass, so the body may run zero times. Testing after the body is how do-while works.
Multiplication comes before addition, so x * 2 + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 and case 7 prints seven. nine would need x * (2 + 1).

questions.q: A program must print a table of exactly 10 lines, and the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts. Which loop is normally used for this?
questions.x: The for loop keeps the start value, the test and the update in one line, which suits a known count such as 10. do-while is chosen when the body must run at least once; switch is not a loop at all.

questions.q: A Gantt chart shows four tasks: T1 in weeks 1-3, T2 in weeks 4-6, T3 in weeks 5-8 and T4 in weeks 9-10. Which two tasks are in progress at the same time?
questions.x: T2 runs to week 6 and T3 starts in week 5, so both are under way in weeks 5 and 6. T1 ends in week 3 just before T2 starts in week 4, so those two only meet end to start and do not overlap.

questions.q: Why do software teams follow a Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)?
o: It removes the need to test the software
It lets coding start before anyone knows what is needed
It guarantees that the software has no errors
It divides the work into clear stages that can be planned, checked and managed
questions.x: The SDLC gives a project an ordered set of stages, from requirements to maintenance, so work can be planned and tracked. It includes a testing stage and cannot promise error-free software.

questions.q: A Tkinter program creates `msg = tk.Label(root, text="Welcome")` but never calls `pack()`, `grid()` or `place()` on `msg`. What happens when it runs?
o: The label appears at the top-left corner
The window opens but the label is not shown in it
questions.x: Creating a widget does not display it; a geometry manager (`pack`, `grid` or `place`) must place it in the window. The code is still valid, so there is no error.
`total(2, 3)` returns sq(2) + sq(3) = 4 + 9 = 13. 25 would be (2 + 3) squared, which is not what the code does.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print(not 5 > 3 or 4 > 2)
```
questions.x: Comparisons come first, then `not`, then `or`: `not (5 > 3)` is `not True` = False, and False or (4 > 2) = False or True = True. Applying `not` to the whole line would wrongly give False.

questions.q: Reading the element at a given index of a Python list, such as `L[500]`, takes the same time however long the list is. What is its time complexity?
questions.x: A fixed amount of work, not depending on n, is constant time, O(1). Indexing does not walk through the elements one by one, which would be O(n).

questions.q: The values 30, 10, 45, 5, 20, 40 are inserted, in that order, into an empty binary search tree (smaller values go left, larger go right). What is its in-order traversal (left subtree, node, right subtree)?
questions.x: The in-order traversal of a binary search tree always lists its values in ascending order: 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 45. 30, 10, 5, 20, 45, 40 is the pre-order traversal of the same tree.

questions.q: Four studies test their null hypotheses at α = 0.05 and get the p-values 0.20, 0.04, 0.07 and 0.009. In how many studies is H₀ rejected?
questions.x: H₀ is rejected when p < α: 0.04 and 0.009 are below 0.05, while 0.20 and 0.07 are not. So 2 studies reject H₀; 0.07 is close but still above 0.05.

questions.q: A student searches for `cricket` and then for `cricket AND Lahore`. Compared with the first search, the second search usually returns:
o: fewer results, because each page must contain both words
more results, because two words are searched
the same results in a different order
only pages that contain neither word
questions.x: AND narrows a search: a page must contain cricket and also Lahore, so some cricket pages drop out. It is OR that widens a search.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: Why mercury is more useful than water for building pumps
How weather offices first learned to forecast storms
How a puzzle about pumps led to the discovery that air has weight
Why early scholars refused to accept the results of experiments
questions.x: The passage follows the pump-makers' "awkward fact" to the mercury tube and the idea that water is "pushed up by the weight of the air". Weather is not mentioned at all; the tube is described only as "an instrument for measuring the air itself".

questions.q: According to the passage, what had pump-makers noticed?
o: Their pumps worked better on mountains than in valleys
Water rose faster in narrow pipes than in wide ones
A suction pump could not raise water beyond a certain height
Their pumps lifted mercury more easily than water
questions.x: The first paragraph says a suction pump "could not lift water more than about ten metres". The difference between mountains and valleys was noticed later, in the mercury column, not in pumps.

questions.q: The passage suggests that on a mountain the air presses down:
o: less heavily than in a valley, so it holds up a shorter column
more heavily than in a valley, so it holds up a taller column
with the same force as in a valley, since air weighs the same everywhere
not at all, so the gap at the top of the tube disappears
questions.x: The column balances "the same weight of air", and it "stood lower on a mountain than in a valley"; a shorter column means less weight of air pressing down. A heavier push would give a taller column, the opposite of what was seen.

questions.q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "awkward" most nearly means:
o: clumsy in the way it moves
embarrassing to talk about in company
troublesome because it did not fit the accepted idea
questions.x: The fact is "awkward" because a nature that rushes to fill any gap should lift water to any height, yet pumps stopped at a limit. "Clumsy" is the word's everyday meaning for people, not for a fact.

questions.q: In the second paragraph, the phrase "just as the idea predicted" refers to the prediction that:
o: the mercury would fill the whole tube and leave no gap
a heavier liquid would need a shorter column than water
the column would rise and fall slightly from day to day
the gap at the top of the tube would slowly fill with air
questions.x: The sentence explains the prediction itself: "a heavier liquid needs less height to balance the same weight of air", so the mercury column was "much shorter than ten metres". The daily rise and fall was noticed "soon" afterwards, not predicted.

questions.q: The passage is chiefly an explanation of:
o: why leopards are easy to see in a zoo
how hunters track their prey through forests
several ways in which animals avoid being seen
why octopuses are the most skilled of all animals
questions.x: Camouflage "takes several forms", and the passage describes matching, breaking up the outline, countering shadow and changing appearance. The zoo and the octopus are single examples.

questions.q: What, according to the passage, most often gives a hidden animal away?
questions.x: The last sentence says "Movement, more than colour or shape, is what most often gives a hidden creature away." A hunter is "quick to spot an outline", but movement is named as the commonest giveaway.

questions.q: The passage suggests that a leopard's spots would help it least:
o: while it is lying completely still
on open, evenly lit ground with no shadows
questions.x: The spots work by scattering the outline "among the shadows of a forest floor"; where there are no shadows they have nothing to blend with, and they "seem eye-catching in a zoo". The shady forest floor is where they work best.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "dissolve" most nearly means:
questions.x: The spots "scatter its outline" so the edges can no longer be seen clearly; they fade from view. Mixing into a liquid, as sugar does in water, is the commoner meaning.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the second and third paragraphs?
o: It gives more examples of matching the background
It argues against the methods in the second paragraph
It explains how leopards came to have spots
It moves from tricks of colour and outline to a trick that works on light and shadow
questions.x: The second paragraph covers colour and broken outlines; the third begins "A subtler trick deals with light" and explains the pale belly that "cancels the shadow". It adds a method rather than arguing against the earlier ones.
